title: Chat System
subtitle: Real-time messaging architecture: stateful WebSockets, hybrid group fan-out, and offline inbox synchronization.
keyTakeaways: Maintain persistent, stateful bidirectional WebSocket connections on gateway nodes, backed by a Redis Session Registry mapping userId -> gatewayNodeId for cross-server message routing.
Use per-conversation monotonic sequence numbers (or Snowflake IDs) as clustering keys in Cassandra (channel_id, message_id) so clients can order messages and sync missed history reliably.

Apply hybrid fan-out for group chats: push to each member's inbox/connection for small groups (<= 500 members), and use message-bus pub/sub for massive channels with thousands of concurrent listeners.

sections.heading: 1. Requirements Engineering & Scope Boundaries
sections.body: A real-time Chat System supports 1-on-1 private messaging, multi-user group chats, delivery receipts, and seamless offline history synchronization across multiple devices.
bullets: Functional: Low-latency 1-on-1 and group messaging; online/offline presence indicators; delivery and read receipts (sent, delivered, read).
Functional: Multi-device synchronization and offline message delivery when users reconnect.
Non-Functional: Sub-100ms message delivery latency for online recipients globally.
Non-Functional: Strict message ordering per conversation: messages must never display out of sequence.
Non-Functional: High availability with zero message loss once accepted by the server.
Out of Scope: End-to-end encryption key exchange protocols, voice/video VoIP calling, and large file storage.

sections.heading: 2. Traffic Modeling & Workload Assumptions
sections.body: Messaging systems maintain millions of persistent, idle socket connections while processing high-volume short-text messages.
bullets: User Base: 50 million daily active users (DAU) sending an average of 40 messages per day = 2 billion messages/day (~23,000 messages/second average, peaking at 75,000 msg/sec).
Concurrent Connections: 10 million concurrent active WebSocket connections during peak hours.
Message Payload: Average message is ~200 bytes of text and metadata. 2 billion messages * 200 bytes = 400 GB/day of persistent message data.
Gateway Capacity: A tuned Linux server (Netty/epoll) can hold ~50,000 to 100,000 idle WebSocket connections. 10 million connections require 100 to 200 gateway instances.

sections.heading: 3. Back-of-the-Envelope Capacity Calculations
sections.body: Sizing chat infrastructure involves budgeting for persistent socket memory, message queue throughput, and long-term history storage.
bullets: Socket memory sizing: A single idle WebSocket connection consumes ~10 to 30 KB of OS kernel buffer and application memory. 100,000 connections per server require ~2 to 3 GB of RAM, meaning gateway nodes are typically CPU- or file-descriptor-bound rather than memory-bound.
Storage retention: 400 GB/day * 365 days = 146 TB per year. Stored in Cassandra with replication factor 3 = ~438 TB of disk across the storage cluster.
Bandwidth requirements: 75,000 peak msgs/sec * 200 bytes = 15 MB/s of ingress traffic, expanding to 60 MB/s outbound due to group chat fan-out.

================================================================================
                     CHAT SYSTEM CAPACITY ESTIMATION SHEET
================================================================================
1. MESSAGE & PRESENCE QPS (100M DAU, 50M Concurrent Connections)
   - Daily Messages Sent        : 4,000,000,000 (4B / day)
   - Average Write QPS          : 4B / 86,400        = ~46,300 QPS
   - Peak Write QPS (3x)        : 46,300 * 3         = ~140,000 QPS
   - Daily Fan-Out Deliveries   : 16,000,000,000 (16B / day, avg 4 recipients)
   - Average Delivery QPS       : 16B / 86,400       = ~185,200 QPS
   - Peak Delivery QPS (3x)     : 185,200 * 3        = ~555,000 QPS
   - Presence Heartbeat QPS     : 50M CCU / 30 sec   = ~1,666,667 Pings/sec

2. WEBSOCKET GATEWAY & REDIS MEMORY (RAM)
   - Concurrent WebSockets      : 50M users * 1.2 avg devices = 60M open sockets
   - Memory per Socket (Netty)  : ~15 KB (TCP + TLS + Direct Buffer)
   - Gateway Fleet Size         : 60M / 100K sockets per node = 600 Gateway Nodes
   - Redis Session Registry     : 50M users * 200 Bytes       = 10 GB RAM
   - Redis Group Membership     : 50M groups * 500 Bytes      = 25 GB RAM
   - Total Redis Cluster RAM    : ~50 GB Primary (100 GB with 1x Replica)

3. 5-YEAR PERSISTENT STORAGE (Apache Cassandra / ScyllaDB)
   - Daily Message Storage      : 4B msgs/day * 500 Bytes     = 2.0 TB / day
   - 5-Year Raw Message Storage : 2.0 TB/day * 365 * 5        = 3,650 TB (3.65 PB)
   - 5-Year Replicated (RF=3)   : 3.65 PB * 3                 = ~10.95 PB (~11 PB)

4. NETWORK BANDWIDTH
   - Peak Chat Ingress          : 140K QPS * 500B             = 70.0 MB/sec
   - Peak Chat Egress           : 555K QPS * 500B             = 277.5 MB/sec
   - Heartbeat Ping/Pong        : 1.67M QPS * 64B             = 106.7 MB/sec
   - Total Peak Bandwidth       : ~454 MB/sec (~3.63 Gbps)
================================================================================

sections.heading: 4. API Interface Contracts & Data Domain Models
sections.body: Bidirectional communication uses WebSockets for real-time traffic, backed by REST/gRPC endpoints for authentication, file uploads, and history queries.
bullets: WebSocket framing: Compact JSON or Protobuf frames for `SEND_MSG`, `ACK`, `TYPING`, and `READ_RECEIPT`.
REST History API: `GET /v1/channels/{channelId}/messages?lastMessageId=108234&limit=50`.

Storage Schema (Cassandra): Partition Key: `channel_id`, Clustering Key: `message_id DESC`. This layout stores all messages for a conversation together on disk in reverse chronological order, making pagination instant.

sections.heading: 5. High-Level Architecture Blueprint & Component Topology
sections.body: The chat architecture decouples stateful connection maintenance from stateless message routing and storage persistence.
bullets: WebSocket Gateway Fleet: Terminates TLS, maintains long-lived client socket connections, and forwards incoming messages to internal brokers.
Session Registry (Redis Cluster): Tracks user location mapping `userId -> gatewayServerId`, enabling any gateway to locate the server hosting a recipient.
Message Router & Fan-Out Service: Resolves conversation participants, routes 1-on-1 messages, and dispatches group messages.
Distributed Message Store (Cassandra / ScyllaDB): Appends messages to wide-column storage optimized for sequential time-series writes.
Push Notification Service (APNs / FCM): Wakes offline mobile devices when messages arrive while their WebSocket connection is closed.

sections.heading: 6. Deep-Dive Execution Flows & Core Logic
sections.body: Delivering a message reliably requires coordinating between session registries, local sockets, and offline queues.
bullets: 1-on-1 message delivery flow: User A sends a message to User B over their WebSocket to Gateway 1. Gateway 1 queries Redis to find User B's location. Redis reports User B is connected to Gateway 4. Gateway 1 forwards the message over internal RPC to Gateway 4, which pushes it down User B's socket.
Recipient is offline: If Redis reports User B has no active session, the router stores the message in Cassandra and immediately triggers a push notification via APNs/FCM.

Offline synchronization: When User B reconnects, their client issues `GET /sync?since_message_id=X`. The server queries Cassandra (`WHERE channel_id = Y AND message_id > X`) and returns missed messages in order.

sections.heading: 7. Production Hardening, Fault Tolerance & Resilience
sections.body: Handling reconnect stampedes, message deduplication, and server crashes gracefully ensures chat platform stability.
bullets: Reconnect Thundering Herds: When a gateway node crashes, 100,000 clients disconnect and attempt to reconnect simultaneously. Enforce exponential backoff with full jitter on client reconnect logic to prevent gateway collapse.

Message deduplication: Clients generate a unique client-side UUID (`client_msg_id`) before sending. If network drops prevent the sender from receiving an ACK, retrying with the same `client_msg_id` allows the server to deduplicate and prevent double-posting.

Heartbeats and dead connection cleanup: Clients send ping/pong frames every 30 seconds. If a gateway misses two consecutive heartbeats, it terminates the socket and cleans up the session entry in Redis.

tradeOffs.option: Stateful WebSocket Gateways with Redis Session Registry
tradeOffs.pros: Ultra-low latency (<20ms); bidirectional streaming; minimal network packet overhead compared to polling.
tradeOffs.cons: Stateful servers complicate rolling deployments and require connection draining and reconnect management.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Core chat applications (WhatsApp, Slack, Discord) where real-time typing and instant delivery are critical.

tradeOffs.pros: Stateless HTTP infrastructure; simple load balancing with standard reverse proxies.
tradeOffs.cons: Higher latency; extra HTTP header overhead on every message; clumsy client-to-server upstream communication.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Dashboard notifications, live sports scoreboards, and read-only event feeds.

tradeOffs.option: Wide-Column Cassandra vs Relational SQL Storage
tradeOffs.pros: High write throughput; linear horizontal scalability; natural chronological clustering by message ID.
tradeOffs.cons: Does not support complex SQL joins or secondary index queries; requires strict query-driven schema modeling.
tradeOffs.bestFor: High-volume message storage and chronological timeline feeds.

interviewTip: When asked how messages are routed between users, walk through the Redis Session Registry: User A's gateway checks Redis for User B's server ID and forwards the message internally. Explain how Cassandra clustering keys (channel_id, message_id) provide deterministic ordering and simple offline history sync.
